title: Mira's last visit at Dwarka
hookLine: asked to come home, Mira goes in to take leave of her Lord at Dwarka, and stays
carry: the Lord is present in the murti
last: A BHAJAN SINGS IN A SAINT'S FOOTSTEPS.

cards: A delegation from home stands at the door. They've traveled a long way, to a temple town by the sea on the far western coast. They've been sent to bring a woman back, and they aren't supposed to return without her.
She listens. She doesn't say no. She asks for one thing first: let me go to the temple once more.
The town is Dwarka, the city tradition gives to Krishna in his later life. The woman is Mira, and today, our last day with her, is the story tradition tells of how her road ended.

teach.b: This is tradition's story, in paraphrase. After Vrindavan, Mira travels on to Dwarka, the city of Krishna as a king, where he is worshipped in the temple as Ranchhod.
Back in Mewar, things have gone badly, and some tellings say the royal house comes to believe its troubles began when Mira was driven out. So messengers are sent to bring her home.
They plead; some tellings say they threaten to fast until she agrees.

teach.h: ONE LAST VISIT, ONLY HER SARI LEFT
teach.b: Mira asks only to go into the temple first, to take leave of her Lord. She goes in, and she doesn't come out. Tradition says she merged into the image of Krishna, and that her sari was found wrapped around it.
Why ask to go in first? Because for a devotee, the image in that temple isn't a statue of Krishna.

teach.h: THE LORD IS PRESENT IN THE MURTI
teach.b: It's a murti, and Hindus believe that once a murti is installed and invited with prayer, the Lord is present in it. That's why temples wake the deity at dawn, bathe him, dress him and offer him food.
Mira wasn't saying goodbye to a building. She was taking leave of her Lord, the way you'd hold someone before a long trip.

And the tradition tells what happened next as union, not death. Andal's story, a few days ago, ends almost the same way, at Srirangam. Two women, two languages, and both go into the shrine to the Lord who is there.
That is why, in many Hindu homes today, people stop at the shrine before a long trip: you take leave of someone who is there.

how: Pilgrims to Krishna's temple at Dwarka hear the story of Mira's last visit, and devotees remember her with her songs at Dwarka, in Vrindavan and in Rajasthan.

o: a poet whose road, tradition says, ended in Krishna
a poet who left Dwarka by sea and was never found
a poet who went back to Mewar and ruled as a queen

games.q: you're Mira, at Dwarka. messengers from your husband's family plead with you to come home, and won't leave without you. what do you do?
o: ask to visit the temple one last time.
games.why: she asks for one more visit to her Lord, present in the temple murti. she goes in and doesn't come out; tradition says she merged into Krishna's image.

practice: Many Hindu families bow to the home shrine before they leave the house, and again when they come back: palms together, darshan, seeing the Lord and being seen.

If there's a murti or a picture near you, stand before it and greet it as someone present, not an object, and say where you're going today. If you don't pray, pause at your door and bring to mind who you'll come home to.

wordCard.voice: Mirabai. Asked to come home, she went into the Dwarka temple for one last visit, and only her sari was found, wrapped around Krishna's image.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Dwarka, Krishna's city by the sea, where tradition says Mira's road ended.

carryVoice: Your line: the Lord is present in the murti. Mira went in to say goodbye to him, and stayed. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Hagiographical tradition of Mirabai: the messengers at Dwarka and her merging into the image
Hindu temple and home worship: the deity present in the installed murti (prana pratishtha), daily waking, bathing, dressing and feeding, darshan
